clue.text: Jazz genre's providing hits

parts.note: bop (bebop) is a style of jazz
the possessive S, read as a letter

explanation.surface: A music writer claims a jazz style is producing chart hits.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'hits' sound like chart successes; here it is the verb-noun for blows, which is what bops are.
explanation.definitionFit: A bop is a punch or blow, so bops are hits.

clue.text: Attacks putting Belgium on edge, son

indicators.note: placing one piece in position beside the next

parts.note: B is the international vehicle code for Belgium
the roadside is the edge of a road

explanation.surface: Military attacks that leave Belgium tense, with a son somehow involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On edge' reads as nervous, but 'on' is the placing word and 'edge' alone gives ROADSIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadside is a full volley of fire, or a fierce verbal attack.

clue.text: Camera-loving, goofy pooch: get in!

indicators.note: silly and clumsy, so the letters are in a foolish order

explanation.surface: An owner calls a silly, camera-hogging dog back indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog and the camera belong together in the picture, which hides that 'pooch get in' is simply letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Something photogenic looks good on camera, as if the camera loves it.

clue.text: In France, thousands mobbing idiot in city on the Med

indicators.note: tells you to take the French word

parts.note: mille is French for thousand; plural MILLES
an arse is British slang for a fool

explanation.surface: A crowd of thousands hounds a fool in a Mediterranean city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In France' looks like it locates the city, but it tells you to translate 'thousands'. The English spelling of the city keeps the final S that the French Marseille drops.
explanation.definitionFit: Marseilles is France's great port on the Mediterranean.

clue.text: Having lost front of tome, fussily laminate one on bookshelves

definitions.note: an author whose books stand on many bookshelves

indicators.note: the word laminate has lost a letter before its letters are reworked
fussily suggests fiddling about, so the remaining letters are rearranged
the front of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A fussy bookbinder laminates a damaged volume missing its front cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having lost' the T at the 'front of tome', LAMINATE leaves LAMINAE, which 'fussily' rearranges. A A Milne wrote Winnie-the-Pooh.
explanation.definitionFit: A A Milne, author of Winnie-the-Pooh, is a writer whose books are found on shelves everywhere.

clue.text: Medical supports after run's undergone change of direction

indicators.note: right becomes left: the R for right is swapped for an L for left

parts.note: sprint's, a run's, written as sprints

explanation.surface: After a run goes badly, an injured athlete needs medical supports.
explanation.walkthrough: SPRINTS (run's) has its R, the abbreviation for right, changed to L for left: a 'change of direction'.
explanation.definitionFit: Splints are rigid strips strapped to a broken limb to hold it still while it heals.

clue.text: Ivanhoe, novel: almost perfect? Beats me!

indicators.note: novel means new and different, so the letters of Ivanhoe are put in a new order
almost means the final letter is left off

explanation.surface: A reader judges Walter Scott's Ivanhoe close to perfect, then admits being baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a description of Ivanhoe, but it signals a rearrangement, giving IHAVENO; IDEAL, 'almost' complete, is IDEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Beats me is an informal way of saying you cannot think of an answer at all.

clue.text: In report, vegetable that's prepared by whistleblower

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the noun it describes: something prepared by a whistleblower

indicators.note: a report is something spoken and heard, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: the leek is a long onion-family vegetable

explanation.surface: A news report about a vegetable dish prepared by a whistleblower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prepared' pulls toward cooking the vegetable; the whistleblower prepares a leak of documents.
explanation.definitionFit: A whistleblower releases secret information, which is a leak.

clue.text: Second time Everyman's shown up: stop!

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' turns the piece to read bottom to top

parts.note: the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as ME

explanation.surface: The second time the crossword setter has appeared, someone cries stop.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter naming himself stands for ME, and this ME reads upward as EM.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as an imperative verb: you stem bleeding or a tide by halting its flow.

clue.text: Woodwind member regularly going for broke

indicators.note: taking every other letter

parts.note: the even letters of fOr BrOkE

explanation.surface: A woodwind player keeps going all out for broke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going for broke' reads as a single idiom, but 'going' belongs to the indicator and only 'for broke' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the double-reed oboe sits in the orchestra's woodwind section alongside flute and clarinet.

clue.text: Bring together, in the morning, bits of seaweed, pal

parts.note: an alga is one of the simple plants that make up seaweed

explanation.surface: Instructions to gather seaweed with a friend on a morning beach walk.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make the clue read as a list of things to collect; each item is simply the next piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: merging companies or metals into one whole is uniting them.

clue.text: Omit one of the Soup Dragon's friends: goof!

parts.words: one of the Soup Dragon's friends
parts.note: the Soup Dragon lives with the Clangers, so one of them is a Clanger

explanation.surface: Leave out one of a children's-TV character's friends, which would be a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: The Clangers was a British children's TV show about small knitted creatures on a planet with the Soup Dragon. To drop a clanger is British slang for making an embarrassing mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: Dropping a clanger means committing an obvious blunder, a goof.

clue.text: An inspiration? Bold old university radical getting dainty snack

parts.note: a muse is a source of inspiration

explanation.surface: A bold old campus radical, once an inspiration, is now handed a tiny appetiser.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark makes 'An inspiration?' look like a comment; it is the first piece, A MUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: An amuse-bouche is a bite-sized appetiser served before a meal.

clue.text: Puddings, good and bad consumed: nice feelings later

indicators.note: eaten up, so the outer word takes the others inside

parts.note: afters is British slang for dessert
low = poor, bad, as in low quality

explanation.surface: Puddings good and bad were eaten, and a warm contented feeling followed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good and bad' sounds like a verdict on the puddings, but each word is a piece to be swallowed. In Britain 'pudding' and 'afters' both mean dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: An afterglow is the pleasant feeling left once something is over.

clue.text: Misguided idealist embracing 'alternative' leaders

definitions.note: a leader in a newspaper is its main opinion article

indicators.note: the jumbled letters wrap around the alternative word
misguided means led astray, so the letters of idealist are rearranged

explanation.surface: A misguided idealist follows alternative political leaders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misguided' rearranges IDEALIST to EDITIALS, 'embracing' OR. 'leaders' are not people here but leading articles in newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: A leader, or leading article, is the newspaper piece giving the paper's own opinion, which is an editorial.

clue.text: Kill 27? With tongs — that's cold

definitions.note: a cryptic hint describing the thing, rather than a synonym

parts.note: to ice someone is slang for to kill them

explanation.surface: A gangster's order to kill, with tongs as the grim tool, called cold-blooded.
explanation.walkthrough: '27' looks like a reference to another clue, but the puzzle has no 27; it is just the number, a cube.
explanation.definitionFit: A description rather than a synonym: tongs are what you use to drop cubes into a drink, and 'that's cold' completes the picture.

clue.text: Dined and jeered

definitions.meaning: to scoff is British slang for to eat greedily
to scoff at is to mock

explanation.surface: Someone ate and then mocked the host.
explanation.walkthrough: Scoff meaning to wolf down food is British informal usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoffed means both ate greedily and mocked.

clue.text: Extremely vicious, insidious look expressing your enmity, primarily?

definitions.text: Extremely vicious, insidious look expressing your enmity, primarily?

indicators.note: take the first letter of each word

parts.words: Extremely vicious, insidious look expressing your enmity
parts.note: first letters of the seven words

explanation.surface: A description of a hostile, malicious glare.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: its first letters spell the answer, and it describes an evil eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The evil eye is a malevolent look believed to cause harm.

clue.text: Lengthily describe one-time currency

explanation.surface: Someone gives a long account of an old currency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One-time currency' reads as a single dead money such as the franc, but the pound is still in use; 'one-time' is its own piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To expound is to explain something in detail.

clue.text: Some yeti dies, tragically, being extremely trim

indicators.note: only part of the following words is used

explanation.surface: A sad scene: a yeti dies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tragically' looks like an anagram indicator, but it only supplies the final T.
explanation.definitionFit: Tidiest is the superlative of tidy, so extremely trim and neat.

clue.text: Novelist to clasp — but regularly dropping — chihuahua?

indicators.note: every other letter is dropped

parts.note: cLaSp, with c, a and p dropped
a chihuahua is a toy dog breed

explanation.surface: A novelist cuddling a tiny dog, which keeps slipping from his grasp.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes make 'regularly dropping' look like the dog wriggling; it applies to 'clasp'. The question mark flags a chihuahua as an example of a toy.
explanation.definitionFit: Leo Tolstoy wrote War and Peace.

clue.text: Ghastly Double German?

definitions.meaning: the surface reads this as a dreadful look-alike; the setter means a ghostly double, a spectral twin
the surface makes it the person's nationality; it says the word for this spectre is itself German

explanation.surface: Someone meets an eerie look-alike of a German.
explanation.walkthrough: The word itself is German, doppel (double) plus Gänger (walker), so 'German' describes the word, not the person.
explanation.definitionFit: A doppelganger is a ghostly or uncanny double of a living person.

clue.text: Dairy product with drug additive: for what reason?

indicators.note: joining the drug to the other piece
added into the other word

explanation.surface: Someone asks why a dairy product has a drug added to it.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes 'for what reason?' look like a puzzled aside about the additive; it is the word the drug is slipped into. E for ecstasy is a standard crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Whey is the watery part left when milk curdles.

clue.text: Herb cycling for a long time

definitions.note: ages, as in 'I waited ages', works adverbially for a long while

indicators.note: cycling sends the first letter round to the end of the word

explanation.surface: A herb has been going round in circles for ages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' moves the S of SAGE from the front to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Ages, used informally as in 'it took ages', means a very long while.

clue.text: Drunk romances eminent lawyers

parts.note: to court someone is to woo them

explanation.surface: A drunk woos distinguished lawyers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' can look like an anagram indicator, but there is nothing here to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The High Courts are senior courts, bodies of eminent judges.

clue.text: Star in river's reflection

indicators.note: a mirror image reads backwards

parts.note: the Avon is a British river

explanation.surface: A star seen mirrored in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Avon is the river through Stratford; reversed it gives NOVA.
explanation.definitionFit: A nova is a star that suddenly flares in brightness.

clue.text: Indeed, strayed wildly in times gone by

parts.note: yes is an affirmation, like indeed

indicators.note: wildly means in a disorderly way, so the letters of strayed are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone confirms that they really did wander off course in the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strayed wildly' reads like part of the story, but 'wildly' is the anagram signal working on 'strayed', and 'in' is just a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Yesterdays, in the plural, are past days, the former times of one's life.

clue.text: Demands chores when temperature's dropped

indicators.note: something dropped is let fall and lost

explanation.surface: When the weather cools, someone demands more household chores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Temperature's dropped' sounds like weather, but it means the letter T is taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as a verb: someone who asks a price or a favour is demanding it.
